children: The great auk was a flightless bird of the alcid family that became extinct in the mid-19th century. It was the only modern species in the genus Pinguinus. The eggs, unusual looking, white, mottled with black marmoreal markings featured a rather unique pointed oval shape. They became an expensive and prized acquisition for ornithologists and other collectors, which prior to the bird’s extinction, contributed to the population’s demise. The bird was flightless and awkward which compounded its vulnerability. Joyce frequently references birds throughout this book, in particular in reference to Stephen. Towards the end of the chapter, Stephen refers to himself as a hawklike man and speaks of his lapwing.

The reference to the auk’s egg here might have a double signification. Firstly this could refer on a visual level to the shape of Stephen’s head. However more importantly, like the auk, Stephen is a rare creature. The sentence, the use of the word ‘meek’ suggests he may, like the bird, be somewhat ungainly, sensitive and susceptible to the other’s who surround him. For example, we get the feeling Buck Mulligan bullies him around somewhat. Yet his intellectual brilliance is unusual and makes him a rare oddity, like the auk, his thoughts, like the eggs of the auk, are prized. His genius is coveted by the others who in their verbal disputes seek to win him over or sway him to their arguments. I cannot help feeling that Stephen represents a young Joyce, an unusually erudite and intelligent young man whose rare brilliance makes him at once overly sensitive yet also makes others crave his company or approval.

children: Lucrece, a legendary Roman housewife whose fate played a vital role in the transition from a Roman Kingdom into a Roman Republic. According to accounts from the Roman historian Livius and the Greek-Roman historian Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Lucretia’s suicide after her rape by an Etruscan king’s son was the immediate cause of the anti-monarchist rebellion that overthrew the monarchy.

The incident kindled the flames of dissatisfaction over the tyrannical methods of the last king of Rome, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus. As a result, the prominent families instituted a republic, drove the Royal Familyfrom Rome. Due to its sheer impact the rape itself became a major theme in European art and literature. Shakespeare penned a narrative poem entitled ‘The Rape of Lucrece’. He made allusion to this poem in some of his other work. He used this idea in Cymbeline (circa 1609–1610). In this play, Iachimo bets Posthumus (Imogen’s husband) that he can make Imogen commit adultery with him. He does not succeed. However, Iachimo convinces Posthumus otherwise using information about Imogen’s bedchamber and body. Iachimo hid in a trunk which was delivered to Imogen’s chamber under the pretence of safekeeping some jewels, a gift for her father, King Cymbeline. The scene in which he emerges from the trunk mimics the scene in The Rape of Lucrece. Indeed, Iachimo compares himself to Tarquin in the scene: “Our Tarquin thus, / Did softly press the rushes ere he waken’d / The chastity he wounded” (2.2.12–14).

children: L'Art d'être grand-père (“The Art of Being a Grandfather”) is a substantial book of poems by Victor Hugo, published in 1877. They were among the last he wrote.

On 13 March 1871, Hugo’s 44-year-old son Charles died of a stroke while riding in a carriage to a farewell dinner for some of Victor’s friends at a restaurant in Bordeaux. Charles’s wife died shortly afterwards, and Victor Hugo became the guardian of their children, Georges and Jeanne Hugo. The poems describe the feelings of a grandfather entrusted with innocent young children. Love and tenderness are celebrated, discipline is discounted; the freshness and laughter of the young soften the potential bleakness of old age. A trip to the zoo sets the poet musing. Many charming scenes are depicted. He keeps up his attack on tyranny and bigotry, and his search for truth.
The English version by Timothy Adès is How to be a Grandfather, Hearing Eye, London 2002. (wikipedia)

children: The Dark Lady of the Sonnets is a 1910 short comedy by George Bernard Shaw in which William Shakespeare, intending to meet the “Dark Lady”, accidentally encounters Queen Elizabeth I and attempts to persuade her to create a national theatre. The play was written as part of a campaign to create a “Shakespeare National Theatre” by 1916.

The Dark Lady is a woman described in Shakespeare’s sonnets (127–152), and so called because the poems make it clear that she has black wiry hair, and dark, “dun”-coloured skin. The description of the Dark Lady distinguishes itself from the Fair Youth sequence by being overtly sexual. Among these, Sonnet 151 has been characterized as “bawdy” and is used to illustrate the difference between the spiritual love for the Fair Youth and the sexual love for the Dark Lady. The distinction is commonly made in the introduction to modern editions of the sonnets. As with the Fair Youth sequence, there have been many attempts to identify her with a real historical individual. A widely held scholarly opinion, however, is that the “dark lady” is nothing more than a construct of Shakespeare’s imagination and art, and any attempt to identify her with a real person is “pointless”.

This particular phrase, answering a query (“what is the word known to all men?”) that occurs in other chapters, appeared as an answer in one of Joyce’s many manuscript versions, then disappeared again, and did not appear in published editions from 1922 to 1984.
This inclusion was criticized by Richard Ellman, but Gabler was still defending it in 2024:
https://books.openbookpublishers.com/10.11647/obp.0325/ch14.xhtml

Do you know what you are talking about? Love, yes. Word known to all men. Amor vero aliquid alicui bonum vult unde et ea quae concupiscimus ...
― James Joyce – Ulysses (Chap. 9 - Scylla and Charybdis)
